\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a curve on a normalised window, in the motivating
case a ratio $R(u) = T(u)/M(u)$ of a measured quantity $T$ to a modelled baseline $M$, so
that $R \equiv 1$ under a perfect model. Empirically $R$ carries a mid-window hump: a
broad excursion to $\approx 1.2$ centred near $u^{*} \approx 0.65$.

A histogram of $f$ depends on two choices: the \textbf{bin width} $w>0$ (equivalently the
bin count $n_b = 1/w$ on a unit window) and the \textbf{grid offset} $o$ (equivalently a
circular shift of the bin boundaries). Both are conventions, not data. A feature that
appears at one $(w,o)$ and disappears at another is a property of the picture; a feature
that is invariant is a property of the curve. Practitioners resolve this by folklore
(``vary $w$; if it survives, believe it''). Our aim is to replace the folklore with
theorems saying exactly which functionals of a histogram are invariant, in which sense,
and with what error constants.

\subsection{The probe}

The empirical design was a full product grid: bin counts
$n_b \in \{10,20,33,50,66,100\}$ crossed with circular grid shifts
$\mathrm{sh} \in \{-0.25,-0.125,0,+0.125,+0.25\}$ (in units of one bin), giving
$6\times 5 = 30$ cells, each a complete re-histogramming of the same curve. Three
registered readouts per cell: presence of a hump, its amplitude, and its location, the
latter two estimated by a three-point local quadratic fit through the argmax bar and its
neighbours. The anchor cell $(n_b=50,\mathrm{sh}=0)$ reproduced an independent prior
computation: raw maximum $1.22636$ against $1.2227$ (difference $0.004$), interior bins
agreeing to $\le 0.005$; the edge bins differ only through a centre-value versus
integrated-value convention for $M$.

\section{Definitions}

Throughout, $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous and $w>0$.

\begin{definition}[Bin average]
For $a\in\mathbb{R}$, $\displaystyle \avg(f;a,w) = \frac{1}{w}\int_a^{a+w} f(x)\,dx$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Grid, bin values, bin centres]
A \emph{grid} is a pair $(o,w)$, $w>0$. Its $i$-th bin value and centre, $i\in\mathbb{Z}$,
are
\[ B_i(o,w) = \avg\big(f;\, o+iw,\, w\big), \qquad c_i(o,w) = o + \Big(i+\tfrac12\Big)w. \]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sliding average]
The \emph{box-kernel sliding average} of $f$ at scale $w$ is
\[ (S_w f)(x) = \frac{1}{w}\int_{x-w/2}^{\,x+w/2} f(s)\,ds
             = \frac{1}{w}\int_{-w/2}^{w/2} f(x+s)\,ds . \]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Three-point quadratic fit]
Given $y_-,y_0,y_+$ at abscissae $x_0-w,\,x_0,\,x_0+w$, write the \emph{discrete
curvature} $D = y_- - 2y_0 + y_+$ and the \emph{neighbour asymmetry} $A = y_- - y_+$.
When $D\ne 0$ the interpolating parabola has
\[ \hat x(x_0,w) = x_0 + \frac{wA}{2D}, \qquad \hat y = y_0 - \frac{(y_+-y_-)^2}{8D}. \]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cone condition]
$f$ has a \emph{$\kappa$-cone peak} at $x_s$ if $f(x) \le f(x_s) - \kappa|x-x_s|$ for all
$x$, with $\kappa>0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Concavity, midpoint form]
$f$ is concave if for all $x,y$ and all $a,b\ge0$ with $a+b=1$,
$a f(x) + b f(y) \le f(ax+by)$.
\end{definition}

\section{The sampling identity and rigid transport}

\begin{theorem}[Sampling identity]\label{thm:sampling}
For every $o\in\mathbb{R}$, $w>0$, $i\in\mathbb{Z}$: $B_i(o,w) = (S_w f)\big(c_i(o,w)\big)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both sides are $w^{-1}$ times the integral of $f$ over an interval of length $w$; the bin
$[o+iw,\,o+iw+w]$ and the window $[c_i-w/2,\,c_i+w/2]$ with $c_i = o+(i+\tfrac12)w$
coincide.
\end{proof}

The offset is thus not a parameter of the statistic. All $30$ cells of the probe are
samples of six functions $S_w f$ taken at five different sets of abscissae each; any
question of the form ``does the feature survive a change of offset?'' concerns sampling
points only.

\begin{theorem}[Data shift equals grid shift]\label{thm:shift}
For all $a,w,t$: $\avg\big(f(\cdot+t);a,w\big) = \avg(f;a+t,w)$. Consequently the $i$-th
bin value of the $t$-translated data on the grid $(o,w)$ equals the $i$-th bin value of
the original data on the grid $(o+t,w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure: $x\mapsto x+t$ carries
$\int_a^{a+w} f(x+t)\,dx$ to $\int_{a+t}^{a+w+t} f(x)\,dx$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rigid transport of centres]\label{thm:centres}
$c_i(o+t,w) = c_i(o,w) + t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Label drift versus absolute invariance]\label{cor:label}
Under a grid shift by $t$ the \emph{index} of the argmax bin changes by construction
(Theorem \ref{thm:shift}), while the \emph{absolute} argmax location transports rigidly
(Theorem \ref{thm:centres}). Hence the bin label plus the shift, not the label alone, is
the candidate invariant.
\end{corollary}

This is precisely the empirical pattern: the reported vertex label drifted with the
shift, while the corrected quantity sat in $[0.6482,0.6492]$ over all five shifts at
$n_b=100$.

\section{The one-sided certificate}

\begin{lemma}[Averages respect pointwise bounds]\label{lem:bounds}
Let $w>0$, $f$ continuous on $[a,a+w]$. If $f\le M$ there then $\avg(f;a,w)\le M$; if
$f\ge M$ there then $\avg(f;a,w)\ge M$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Monotonicity of the integral against the constant $M$, with $\int_a^{a+w} M = wM$, then
divide by $w>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:exists}
For $w>0$ and $f$ continuous there exists $x\in[a,a+w]$ with $\avg(f;a,w)\le f(x)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$[a,a+w]$ is compact and non-empty so $f$ attains a maximum at some $x^\ast$; apply
Lemma \ref{lem:bounds} with $M=f(x^\ast)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One-sided certificate]\label{thm:cert}
Let $f$ be continuous, $w>0$, $o\in\mathbb{R}$, $i\in\mathbb{Z}$ and suppose
$B_i(o,w)\ge c$. Then $f(x)\ge c$ for some $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Lemma \ref{lem:exists} on the bin $[o+iw,\,o+iw+w]$ with the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

Box averaging is a contraction toward the mean: it can only reduce extremes. Therefore no
choice of $(w,o)$ can create amplitude the curve does not possess, while any choice may
destroy it. Hence \emph{the persistence of a raw-max hump across a bin-width $\times$
shift grid is not an artefact hypothesis at all}. For the probe, $30/30$ cells recorded a
raw maximum in $[1.0706,1.2960]$, so the curve certifiably attains at least $1.0706$.
What remains open is calibration, addressed in Section \ref{sec:controls}.

\section{Amplitude is binning-independent}

\begin{theorem}[Lipschitz lower bound]\label{thm:liplow}
Let $L\ge0$ with $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y$. If $c\in[a,a+w]$ then
$f(c) - Lw \le \avg(f;a,w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $x\in[a,a+w]$, $|c-x|\le w$, so $f(x) \ge f(c) - L|c-x| \ge f(c)-Lw$ pointwise on the
bin; apply Lemma \ref{lem:bounds}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Peak bound]\label{thm:peak}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{thm:liplow}, if additionally $f(x)\le f(x_s)$ for all
$x$ and $x_s\in[a,a+w]$, then $\big|\avg(f;a,w)-f(x_s)\big| \le Lw$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Upper bound by Lemma \ref{lem:bounds} with $M=f(x_s)$; lower bound by Theorem
\ref{thm:liplow} with $c=x_s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Every point is binned]\label{lem:binned}
For any $o$, $w>0$, $x_s$ there is $i=\lfloor (x_s-o)/w\rfloor$ with
$x_s\in[o+iw,\,o+iw+w]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Width independence of the raw maximum]\label{thm:width}
Let $f$ be continuous and $L$-Lipschitz with global maximiser $x_s$. For any two grids
$(o_1,w_1),(o_2,w_2)$ with arbitrary, unrelated offsets there are indices $i,j$ with
\[ \big|B_i(o_1,w_1) - B_j(o_2,w_2)\big| \;\le\; L\,(w_1+w_2). \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose $i,j$ by Lemma \ref{lem:binned} so that $x_s$ lies in bin $i$ of the first grid and
bin $j$ of the second. Theorem \ref{thm:peak} gives $|B_i - f(x_s)|\le Lw_1$ and
$|B_j - f(x_s)|\le Lw_2$; apply the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact deflation for a parabolic hump}

\begin{theorem}[Sliding average of a parabola]\label{thm:parab}
For $c,k,x_s\in\mathbb{R}$, $w>0$ and $f(s)=c-k(s-x_s)^2$,
\[ (S_w f)(x) = c - k\Big[(x-x_s)^2 + \frac{w^2}{12}\Big]. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Split the integral. The constant part contributes $c$. For the quadratic part,
$\int_a^b (s-d)^2 ds = \frac{(b-d)^3-(a-d)^3}{3}$; with $a=x-w/2$, $b=x+w/2$, $d=x_s$ and
$\delta = x-x_s$ this equals $w\delta^2 + w^3/12$. Divide by $w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:parab}
$S_w f$ is a parabola with the same curvature $k$ and the same vertex $x_s$ for every $w$;
$(S_w f)(x_s) = c - kw^2/12$; and
$(S_{w_1}f)(x_s) - (S_{w_2}f)(x_s) = k(w_2^2-w_1^2)/12$.
\end{corollary}

The measured amplitude therefore differs from the true amplitude by a deterministic,
computable quantity $kw^2/12$, identical for every offset. This is the analytic content
of the complaint that ``the estimator is stricter than the phenomenon'': a fixed
amplitude bar applied to a binned curve tests $c - kw^2/12$, not $c$.

\section{Vertex localisation and transport}

\subsection{General case: an $O(w)$ bound with no offset dependence}

\begin{theorem}[Argmax bin near the peak]\label{thm:argmax}
Let $f$ be continuous and $L$-Lipschitz with a $\kappa$-cone peak at $x_s$. Fix any grid
$(o,w)$; let $j$ be the index with $x_s$ in bin $j$, and let $i$ satisfy
$B_j(o,w) \le B_i(o,w)$. Then
\[ \big|c_i(o,w) - x_s\big| \;\le\; \frac{w}{2} + \frac{L}{\kappa}\,w . \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $d=|c_i-x_s|$. Every $x$ in bin $i$ has $|x-c_i|\le w/2$, so by the reverse triangle
inequality $|x-x_s|\ge d-w/2$, and the cone condition gives
$f(x)\le f(x_s)-\kappa(d-w/2)$ on that bin; averaging (Lemma \ref{lem:bounds}) yields
$B_i \le f(x_s)-\kappa(d-w/2)$. Since $x_s$ lies in bin $j$, Theorem \ref{thm:liplow}
gives $B_j \ge f(x_s)-Lw$. Chaining with $B_j\le B_i$ gives $\kappa(d-w/2)\le Lw$.
\end{proof}

The bound contains no offset: the argmax bin's absolute centre lies in a fixed
neighbourhood of $x_s$ of radius $(\tfrac12+L/\kappa)w$ for every shift, shrinking
linearly under refinement.

\subsection{Sharp case: exact rigidity under symmetry and concavity}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry preservation]\label{thm:symm}
If $f(2x_s-x)=f(x)$ for all $x$, then $(S_wf)(2x_s-x)=(S_wf)(x)$ for all $x$ and $w$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Rewrite the integrand over the reflected window using the symmetry, then substitute
$s\mapsto 2x_s-s$, which maps the window onto the original one.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Concavity preservation]\label{thm:conc}
If $f$ is continuous and concave then $S_w f$ is concave for every $w>0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In centred form, for $a,b\ge0$ with $a+b=1$, concavity applied pointwise gives
$a f(x+s) + b f(y+s) \le f(ax+by+s)$ for each $s$ (using $as+bs=s$). Integrate over
$s\in[-w/2,w/2]$ and divide by $w>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Symmetric $+$ concave $\Rightarrow$ radially monotone]\label{lem:unimodal}
Let $g$ be symmetric about $x_s$ and concave. If $|u-x_s|\le|v-x_s|$ then $g(v)\le g(u)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set $t=v-x_s$, $r=u-x_s$. If $t=0$ then $r=0$ and the claim is trivial. Otherwise
$|r/t|\le1$; put $\lambda = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{r}{2t}\in[0,1]$, so that
$\lambda(x_s+t) + (1-\lambda)(x_s-t) = u$. Concavity gives
$\lambda g(x_s+t) + (1-\lambda) g(x_s-t) \le g(u)$, and symmetry gives
$g(x_s-t) = g(x_s+t) = g(v)$; hence $g(v)\le g(u)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact vertex preservation]\label{thm:exactvertex}
If $f$ is continuous, symmetric about $x_s$ and concave, then for every $w>0$ and every
$x$, $(S_wf)(x) \le (S_wf)(x_s)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorems \ref{thm:symm} and \ref{thm:conc} make $S_wf$ symmetric and concave; apply
Lemma \ref{lem:unimodal} with $u=x_s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A single number caps every cell]\label{cor:cap}
Under the same hypotheses, $B_i(o,w) \le (S_wf)(x_s)$ for every offset $o$ and index $i$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Exact rigid transport: the nearest bin wins]\label{thm:nearest}
Under the same hypotheses, for every offset $o$ and indices $i,j$,
\[ |c_i(o,w)-x_s| \le |c_j(o,w)-x_s| \;\Longrightarrow\; B_j(o,w) \le B_i(o,w). \]
Hence for every offset the argmax bin is exactly the bin whose centre is nearest $x_s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem \ref{thm:sampling} converts both bin values to samples of $S_wf$ at the bin
centres; apply Lemma \ref{lem:unimodal} to $g=S_wf$.
\end{proof}

The argmax bin is therefore determined by pure geometry, and the residual spread across
shifts measures the curve's departure from exact symmetry rather than instrument
instability.

\section{Auditing the estimator: the three-point quadratic fit}

\begin{theorem}[The fit never lowers the amplitude]\label{thm:qpeak}
If $D = y_- - 2y_0 + y_+ < 0$ then $\hat y \ge y_0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\hat y - y_0 = -\frac{(y_+-y_-)^2}{8D}$; the numerator is a square and $8D<0$, so the
quotient is $\le 0$.
\end{proof}

Hence a bar of the form ``fitted amplitude $\ge 1.10$'' is \emph{weaker} than ``raw
central value $\ge 1.10$''. The probe's marginals ($22/30$ raw maxima at or above $1.10$
but only $7/30$ fitted amplitudes) cannot be explained by the fit shaving the peak; the
gap must arise upstream, from which bar the pipeline supplied as $y_0$, or from fits whose
curvature was not strictly negative.

\begin{theorem}[Non-degenerate fits localise the vertex]\label{thm:qvert}
If $y_-\le y_0$, $y_+\le y_0$ and $D<0$, then $|\hat x(x_0,w) - x_0| \le w/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\hat x - x_0 = \frac{wA}{2D}$ with $A=y_--y_+$ and $-D = 2y_0-y_--y_+>0$. Then
$-D-A = 2(y_0-y_-) \ge 0$ and $-D+A = 2(y_0-y_+) \ge 0$, so $|A|\le -D$ and
$|wA/(2D)| = w|A|/(2|D|) \le w/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A far vertex certifies a degenerate fit]\label{thm:degen}
If $D<0$ and $|\hat x(x_0,w) - x_0| > w/2$, then $|y_--y_+| > -D = |D|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Contrapositive of Theorem \ref{thm:qvert}: if $|A|\le-D$ then $-D-A = 2(y_0-y_-)\ge0$ and
$-D+A = 2(y_0-y_+)\ge0$, i.e.\ $y_-\le y_0$ and $y_+\le y_0$, so
$|\hat x - x_0|\le w/2$.
\end{proof}

The single erratic cell --- $n_b=33$, fitted vertex $0.19$ away while its own argmax bin
centre was $0.01$ from the consensus --- is therefore certified to have had neighbour
asymmetry exceeding curvature: an ill-conditioned three-point fit, not an unstable
feature. A pipeline filtering on $|A|\le|D|$ would have excluded the cell a priori.

\section{Auditing the controls: thresholds must know the bin count}\label{sec:controls}

\begin{theorem}[A flat threshold loses control under refinement]\label{thm:flat}
Suppose each of $n$ bins independently exceeds a fixed level with probability
$p\in(0,1]$. Then the probability that at least one exceeds it is $1-(1-p)^n$, and
$\lim_{n\to\infty}\big(1-(1-p)^n\big)=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$|1-p|<1$, so $(1-p)^n\to0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The bin-count-aware threshold controls the family-wise error]\label{thm:aware}
For any $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and any $n\in\mathbb{N}$,
$1 - \big(1-\tfrac{\alpha}{n}\big)^{n} \le \alpha$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $n=0$ the left side is $0\le\alpha$. For $n\ge1$, $\alpha/n\le1$ so $-\alpha/n\ge-2$
and Bernoulli's inequality gives $(1-\alpha/n)^n \ge 1 + n(-\alpha/n) = 1-\alpha$.
\end{proof}

A bin-count-agnostic bar is thus guaranteed to be breached once the grid is fine enough,
purely by extreme-value behaviour, whatever the data. With $\alpha=0.05$ and $n=100$ the
aware ceiling is $1.05$; the observed breaches at $1.0215$--$1.0305$, corresponding to
two-sided multinomial extremes at $z\approx+3.05$ and $z\approx-3.45$ for
$n\in\{50,66,100\}$, sit strictly inside it. The mechanical verdict string is retained as
an audit record --- it is the honest output of the rule as pre-registered --- but its leak
semantics are falsified: the same cells exhibit both hump persistence (Theorem
\ref{thm:cert}) and rigid vertex transport (Theorems \ref{thm:argmax}, \ref{thm:nearest}),
which a binning artefact cannot produce.

\section{Reinterpreting the probe}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Hump persistence, $30/30$.} Not an artefact candidate: by Theorem
\ref{thm:cert} each reading certifies the curve attains that value; the ``vanish''
precondition was unmet in $0/30$ cells, as the certificate plus Corollary \ref{cor:parab}
predict at the observed widths.
\item \textbf{Absolute vertex $0.6482$--$0.6492$.} Predicted by Corollary \ref{cor:label}
with Theorems \ref{thm:argmax} and \ref{thm:nearest}. At $w=0.01$, Theorem
\ref{thm:nearest} bounds the argmax-centre displacement by $w/2 = 0.005$; the observed
spread of $0.001$ is well inside this.
\item \textbf{Anchor reproduction.} Difference $0.004$ with interior bins to $\le0.005$;
Theorem \ref{thm:width} with $w_1=w_2=0.02$ bounds the expected cross-implementation
discrepancy by $L(w_1+w_2)$, of the observed order for a curve of moderate slope.
\item \textbf{The erratic $n_b=33$ fit.} Certified degenerate by Theorem \ref{thm:degen}.
\item \textbf{Amplitude bar $7/30$ against raw $22/30$.} By Theorem \ref{thm:qpeak} the
fit cannot be the cause; the defect is in the bar's construction.
\item \textbf{Three breaches of the flat $1.02$ bar.} Expected by Theorem \ref{thm:flat};
inside the aware $1.05$ ceiling of Theorem \ref{thm:aware}.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent\textbf{Verdict.} A stable geometric window feature at $u^{*}\approx0.65$. What
was refuted is a specific operationalisation of significance --- a fitted-apex amplitude
bar at $1.10$ required to hold in $80\%$ of cells, achieved in $0/30$ when conjoined with
the vertex and shape bars. The geometry channel remains open; no breakthrough is claimed.

Two pre-grid amendments are recorded for completeness: the treatment baseline $M$ was
replaced by a mixture-Dickman model after a spurious edge peak of $R=1.49$ in bin $0$
under the previous convention, and the control denominator was replaced by a
uniform-sampling null after the previous control produced a manufactured shape of
amplitude $1.3611$. Both amendments preceded the grid run; no registered bar was altered.
Uncertainty used a cluster bootstrap with $2000$ replicates at a single seed. The analysis
is pure reanalysis of stored curves; no new sampling was performed.

\section{A parameter-free shape test}

\begin{theorem}[Discrete curvature sign certificate]\label{thm:curvsign}
Let $f$ be continuous and concave, $w>0$. Then for every $x$,
\[ (S_wf)(x+w) - 2(S_wf)(x) + (S_wf)(x-w) \le 0, \]
and consequently, for every offset $o$ and index $i$,
$B_{i+1}(o,w) - 2B_i(o,w) + B_{i-1}(o,w) \le 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Concavity of $S_wf$ (Theorem \ref{thm:conc}) at the midpoint gives
$\tfrac12(S_wf)(x+w) + \tfrac12(S_wf)(x-w) \le (S_wf)(x)$. For the histogram form, note
$c_{i\pm1}(o,w) = c_i(o,w)\pm w$ and apply Theorem \ref{thm:sampling}.
\end{proof}

This shape test has no fitted parameter: the sign of the second difference of consecutive
bar heights is a faithful readout of local concavity, valid for every bin width and offset
simultaneously, and it cannot suffer the degeneracy of the $n_b=33$ cell because there is
no denominator.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What is invariant, and in what sense}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Quantity & Offset dependence & Width dependence \\
\midrule
Existence of a bar $\ge c$ & none needed & none needed \\
Amplitude & none beyond sampling & $O(Lw)$; exactly $kw^2/12$ for a parabola \\
Argmax bin label & drifts by construction & changes with $w$ \\
Argmax bin centre & transports rigidly & within $w/2 + (L/\kappa)w$ of $x_s$ \\
Second difference sign & none & none for concave $f$ \\
Fitted apex height & inherits sampling; $\ge y_0$ & fit bias \\
Fitted apex position & degenerate if $|A|>|D|$ & as above \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Functionals with no free parameters (existence, amplitude, centre, curvature sign) are
invariant, or invariant up to computable bias. Functionals introduced by the estimator
(fitted apex, flat threshold) are the ones that fail, and they fail in characterisable
ways.

\subsection{Methodological reading}

The folk rule ``vary the bin width'' is vindicated with a precise justification: the
one-sided certificate makes survival meaningful, and rigid transport makes positional
agreement \emph{in absolute coordinates} meaningful. The rule's usual failure mode is also
identified: comparing bin labels instead of absolute positions, then reporting the drift
that Theorem \ref{thm:shift} guarantees as instability.

More generally, the episode illustrates a failure mode of mechanically registered analysis
chains. Every individual rule was defensible; the composition emitted
``artefact-contaminated'' because one rule had the wrong asymptotic form in $n$.
Pre-registration protects against post hoc bar-shifting; it does not protect against a bar
mathematically incapable of controlling what it claims to control. The remedy is to require
that each registered threshold carry a proof of its own validity at the resolutions it will
be applied to --- Theorem \ref{thm:aware} rather than a flat constant.

\subsection{Limitations}

The sharp results assume exact symmetry and concavity near the peak; the observed feature
is only approximately symmetric, so the general $O(w)$ bound is the honest one for the
data. The constants $L$ and $\kappa$ are not estimated here, and converting Theorems
\ref{thm:width} and \ref{thm:argmax} into numerical error bars requires them. The
extreme-value calibration uses an independence approximation across bins, exact only
asymptotically for multinomial counts, and the source bootstrap used a single seed.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Curvature-sign certificates for box-averaged windows]
For $f\in C^2$, the second difference of consecutive bin averages of width $w$ equals
$w\cdot(f''\star\Lambda_w)(x)$ for the triangular (Bartlett) kernel $\Lambda_w$, so the
sign pattern of the histogram's discrete curvature is a faithful, unbiased readout of the
sign pattern of $f''$ smoothed at scale $w$ --- with no fitted parameters and hence no fit
degeneracy of the $n_b=33$ kind.
\end{conjecture}

The key insight is that the box average is a convolution, so second-differencing the
histogram commutes with differentiating the curve, turning a fitted-vertex test into a
kernel-smoothing statement with an analytic error term. Theorem \ref{thm:curvsign} is the
sign-only special case for globally concave $f$.

\begin{conjecture}[Exact vertex rigidity beyond symmetry]
The symmetry hypothesis in Theorem \ref{thm:nearest} can be weakened to log-concavity plus
a one-sided skew bound: if $f$ is log-concave and
$|f(x_s+t) - f(x_s-t)| \le \varepsilon t^2$ for all $t$, then the sliding-average vertex
lies within $C\varepsilon w^2$ of $x_s$ --- a second-order, not first-order, transport
error.
\end{conjecture}

The key insight is that the first-order term in the vertex displacement of a box average
is exactly the local skewness, so any curve whose skewness vanishes to second order
inherits quadratic rather than linear vertex rigidity. This would explain the observed
$0.001$ spread at $w=0.01$, an order of magnitude tighter than the first-order prediction
$w/2 = 0.005$.

A third direction combines Theorem \ref{thm:curvsign} with an analytic standard error for
the second difference under the null. Because the statistic is linear in the data with an
explicit kernel, its variance under a uniform-sampling null is computable in closed form,
giving a significance test with no bootstrap, no seed dependence and no fitted curvature
--- the direct replacement for the operationalisation that failed.

\section{Conclusion}

Every histogram bar is a sample of one offset-free function, the box-kernel sliding
average. From that identity the entire invariance structure of a windowed hump follows:
amplitude is certified one-sidedly and can never be manufactured; it is
binning-independent to $O(Lw)$ and exactly $kw^2/12$-deflated for a parabolic peak; vertex
position transports rigidly, to $O(w)$ in general and exactly under symmetry and
concavity. What is not invariant is what the analyst adds: the apex of a three-point fit,
which can only inflate the amplitude and which diverges precisely when neighbour asymmetry
exceeds curvature, and a control threshold that ignores the bin count, whose family-wise
error tends to one under refinement. For the motivating data the conclusion is a clean
separation of phenomenon from instrument: the mid-window feature at $u^{*}\approx0.65$ is
a stable geometric property of the curve, while the pre-registered test failed for reasons
that are now theorems about the test.

Binning-Independent Geometry of a Windowed Hump — numerical demonstrations.

Self-contained (standard library only).  Every function is inlined and type-hinted.

The script demonstrates, numerically, the results of the accompanying paper:

  1. Sampling identity            B_i(o, w) = (S_w f)(c_i(o, w))
  2. One-sided certificate        a bin value >= c forces sup f >= c
  3. Amplitude stability          |avg - f(x_s)| <= L w ; cross-width <= L (w1 + w2)
  4. Exact parabolic deflation    S_w(c - k(x-x_s)^2)(x) = c - k[(x-x_s)^2 + w^2/12]
  5. Vertex transport             absolute argmax centre invariant under grid shift
  6. Quadratic-fit audit          apex >= centre value; far apex <=> degenerate fit
  7. Control-bar audit            flat threshold FWER -> 1 ; aware threshold <= alpha

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The model curve: a mid-window hump at u* = 0.65 on top of a flat baseline.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

U_STAR: float = 0.65
PEAK_AMPLITUDE: float = 1.23          # true value of R at the peak
BASELINE: float = 1.00                # R == 1 under a perfect model
HUMP_WIDTH: float = 0.16              # Gaussian scale of the hump


def ratio_curve(u: float) -> float:
    """The measured-to-modelled ratio R(u) = T(u)/M(u) on the unit window."""
    return BASELINE + (PEAK_AMPLITUDE - BASELINE) * math.exp(
        -0.5 * ((u - U_STAR) / HUMP_WIDTH) ** 2
    )


def parabolic_hump(c: float, k: float, x_s: float) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    """The canonical smooth hump f(x) = c - k (x - x_s)^2."""

    def f(x: float) -> float:
        return c - k * (x - x_s) ** 2

    return f


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core operators: bin average, bin value, bin centre, sliding average.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def integrate(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, n: int = 4096) -> float:
    """Composite Simpson quadrature of f on [a, b] with n (even) panels."""
    if n % 2 == 1:
        n += 1
    if b == a:
        return 0.0
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += (4.0 if i % 2 == 1 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3.0


def bin_avg(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, w: float) -> float:
    """avg(f; a, w) = (1/w) * integral of f over [a, a + w]."""
    return integrate(f, a, a + w) / w


def bin_center(o: float, w: float, i: int) -> float:
    """Centre c_i(o, w) = o + (i + 1/2) w of the i-th bin of the grid (o, w)."""
    return o + (i + 0.5) * w


def bin_value(f: Callable[[float], float], o: float, w: float, i: int) -> float:
    """Bar height B_i(o, w) = avg(f; o + i w, w)."""
    return bin_avg(f, o + i * w, w)


def sliding_avg(f: Callable[[float], float], w: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Box-kernel sliding average (S_w f)(x) = (1/w) * integral over [x-w/2, x+w/2]."""
    return integrate(f, x - w / 2.0, x + w / 2.0) / w


def histogram(
    f: Callable[[float], float], n_bins: int, shift_in_bins: float
) -> Tuple[List[float], List[float]]:
    """Histogram f on the unit window with `n_bins` bins, grid shifted by
    `shift_in_bins` bin-widths.  Returns (bar heights, absolute bin centres)."""
    w = 1.0 / n_bins
    o = shift_in_bins * w
    heights = [bin_value(f, o, w, i) for i in range(n_bins)]
    centers = [bin_center(o, w, i) for i in range(n_bins)]
    return heights, centers


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The three-point local quadratic fit.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def q_vertex(x0: float, w: float, ym: float, y0: float, yp: float) -> float:
    """Vertex abscissa of the parabola through (x0-w, ym), (x0, y0), (x0+w, yp)."""
    d = ym - 2.0 * y0 + yp
    return x0 + w * (ym - yp) / (2.0 * d)


def q_peak(ym: float, y0: float, yp: float) -> float:
    """Vertex ordinate (fitted amplitude) of the same parabola."""
    d = ym - 2.0 * y0 + yp
    return y0 - (yp - ym) ** 2 / (8.0 * d)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The probe grid.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

BIN_COUNTS: Tuple[int, ...] = (10, 20, 33, 50, 66, 100)
SHIFTS: Tuple[float, ...] = (-0.25, -0.125, 0.0, 0.125, 0.25)


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Sampling identity: every bar is a sample of one offset-free function.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_sampling_identity() -> None:
    banner("1. SAMPLING IDENTITY:  B_i(o,w) = (S_w f)(c_i(o,w))")
    worst = 0.0
    for n_bins in BIN_COUNTS:
        for sh in SHIFTS:
            w = 1.0 / n_bins
            o = sh * w
            for i in (0, n_bins // 3, n_bins // 2, n_bins - 1):
                lhs = bin_value(ratio_curve, o, w, i)
                rhs = sliding_avg(ratio_curve, w, bin_center(o, w, i))
                worst = max(worst, abs(lhs - rhs))
    print(f"  cells checked : {len(BIN_COUNTS) * len(SHIFTS)} (4 bars each)")
    print(f"  max |B - S_w| : {worst:.3e}   (0 up to quadrature error)")
    print("  => the grid offset is not a parameter of the statistic, only of")
    print("     the sampling points.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. One-sided certificate: binning cannot manufacture a hump.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_one_sided_certificate() -> None:
    banner("2. ONE-SIDED CERTIFICATE:  a bar >= c forces sup f >= c")
    true_sup = max(ratio_curve(k / 200000.0) for k in range(200001))
    violations = 0
    amplitudes: List[float] = []
    for n_bins in BIN_COUNTS:
        for sh in SHIFTS:
            heights, _ = histogram(ratio_curve, n_bins, sh)
            raw_max = max(heights)
            amplitudes.append(raw_max)
            if raw_max > true_sup + 1e-9:
                violations += 1
    print(f"  true sup f            : {true_sup:.6f}")
    print(f"  raw maxima over 30 cells: min {min(amplitudes):.6f}  "
          f"max {max(amplitudes):.6f}")
    print(f"  cells exceeding sup f : {violations}  (must be 0)")
    print("  => averaging is a contraction toward the mean: it can flatten a")
    print("     hump but never create one.  Persistence is not an artefact.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Amplitude stability under bin width.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def lipschitz_constant(f: Callable[[float], float], n: int = 20000) -> float:
    """Numerical sup |f'| on [0, 1] by finite differences."""
    h = 1.0 / n
    return max(abs(f((i + 1) * h) - f(i * h)) / h for i in range(n))


def demo_amplitude_stability() -> None:
    banner("3. AMPLITUDE STABILITY:  |raw max(w1) - raw max(w2)| <= L (w1 + w2)")
    lip = lipschitz_constant(ratio_curve)
    print(f"  Lipschitz constant L  ~ {lip:.4f}")
    maxima = {}
    for n_bins in BIN_COUNTS:
        heights, _ = histogram(ratio_curve, n_bins, 0.0)
        maxima[n_bins] = max(heights)
    print("\n  n_bins    raw max     bound L*w    deficit vs sup")
    true_sup = max(ratio_curve(k / 200000.0) for k in range(200001))
    for n_bins in BIN_COUNTS:
        w = 1.0 / n_bins
        print(f"  {n_bins:6d}  {maxima[n_bins]:9.6f}   {lip * w:9.6f}    "
              f"{true_sup - maxima[n_bins]:9.6f}")
    worst = 0.0
    for a in BIN_COUNTS:
        for b in BIN_COUNTS:
            gap = abs(maxima[a] - maxima[b])
            bound = lip * (1.0 / a + 1.0 / b)
            worst = max(worst, gap - bound)
    print(f"\n  max (observed gap - theoretical bound) = {worst:.6f}  (must be <= 0)")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Exact deflation for the parabolic hump:  amplitude loss = k w^2 / 12.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_parabolic_deflation() -> None:
    banner("4. EXACT DEFLATION:  S_w(c - k(x-x_s)^2)(x) = c - k[(x-x_s)^2 + w^2/12]")
    c, k = 1.23, 4.0
    f = parabolic_hump(c, k, U_STAR)
    print("  n_bins     S_w f(x_s)   predicted c - k w^2/12     error")
    for n_bins in BIN_COUNTS:
        w = 1.0 / n_bins
        got = sliding_avg(f, w, U_STAR)
        want = c - k * w * w / 12.0
        print(f"  {n_bins:6d}   {got:11.8f}   {want:20.8f}   {abs(got - want):.2e}")
    w1, w2 = 1.0 / 10, 1.0 / 100
    gap = sliding_avg(f, w1, U_STAR) - sliding_avg(f, w2, U_STAR)
    print(f"\n  cross-width gap (w=1/10 vs 1/100): {gap:+.8f}")
    print(f"  closed form k(w2^2 - w1^2)/12     : "
          f"{k * (w2 * w2 - w1 * w1) / 12.0:+.8f}")
    print("  => a deterministic, offset-free deflation, not evidence against")
    print("     the feature.  It can simply be corrected for.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Vertex transport: the label drifts, the absolute position does not.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_vertex_transport() -> None:
    banner("5. VERTEX TRANSPORT:  bin LABEL drifts, ABSOLUTE centre is invariant")
    print("  n_bins   shift    argmax label   label/n_bins   absolute centre")
    for n_bins in (50, 100):
        for sh in SHIFTS:
            heights, centers = histogram(ratio_curve, n_bins, sh)
            j = max(range(n_bins), key=lambda i: heights[i])
            print(f"  {n_bins:6d}  {sh:+6.3f}   {j:12d}   {j / n_bins:12.4f}   "
                  f"{centers[j]:15.4f}")
        located = []
        for sh in SHIFTS:
            heights, centers = histogram(ratio_curve, n_bins, sh)
            j = max(range(n_bins), key=lambda i: heights[i])
            located.append(centers[j])
        w = 1.0 / n_bins
        print(f"         max |centre - u*| = "
              f"{max(abs(x - U_STAR) for x in located):.4f}  (bound w/2 = "
              f"{w / 2:.4f});  spread = {max(located) - min(located):.4f}"
              f"  (bound w = {w:.4f})\n")
    print("  => 'nearest bin wins': the argmax bin is fixed by geometry, so")
    print("     the absolute vertex is pinned while its label must drift.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Auditing the three-point quadratic fit.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_quadratic_fit_audit() -> None:
    banner("6. FIT AUDIT:  apex >= centre value; a far apex certifies degeneracy")
    print("  n_bins  shift   raw y0     fitted apex   apex - y0   |vx - x0| <= w/2 ?")
    n_fit_ge_raw = 0
    n_total = 0
    for n_bins in BIN_COUNTS:
        for sh in SHIFTS:
            heights, centers = histogram(ratio_curve, n_bins, sh)
            j = max(range(1, n_bins - 1), key=lambda i: heights[i])
            ym, y0, yp = heights[j - 1], heights[j], heights[j + 1]
            d = ym - 2.0 * y0 + yp
            if d >= 0.0:
                continue
            w = 1.0 / n_bins
            apex = q_peak(ym, y0, yp)
            vx = q_vertex(centers[j], w, ym, y0, yp)
            ok = abs(vx - centers[j]) <= w / 2.0 + 1e-12
            n_total += 1
            n_fit_ge_raw += int(apex >= y0 - 1e-12)
            if n_bins in (33, 100) and sh in (-0.25, 0.0):
                print(f"  {n_bins:6d} {sh:+6.3f}  {y0:9.6f}  {apex:12.6f}  "
                      f"{apex - y0:+10.6f}   {ok}")
    print(f"\n  concave fits examined            : {n_total}")
    print(f"  fits with apex >= raw centre bar : {n_fit_ge_raw}  (must equal above)")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The model curve: a mid-window hump at u* = 0.65 on top of a flat baseline.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

U_STAR: float = 0.65
PEAK_AMPLITUDE: float = 1.23          # true value of R at the peak
BASELINE: float = 1.00                # R == 1 under a perfect model
HUMP_WIDTH: float = 0.16              # Gaussian scale of the hump


def ratio_curve(u: float) -> float:
    """The measured-to-modelled ratio R(u) = T(u)/M(u) on the unit window."""
    return BASELINE + (PEAK_AMPLITUDE - BASELINE) * math.exp(
        -0.5 * ((u - U_STAR) / HUMP_WIDTH) ** 2
    )


def parabolic_hump(c: float, k: float, x_s: float) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    """The canonical smooth hump f(x) = c - k (x - x_s)^2."""

    def f(x: float) -> float:
        return c - k * (x - x_s) ** 2

    return f


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core operators: bin average, bin value, bin centre, sliding average.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def integrate(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, n: int = 4096) -> float:
    """Composite Simpson quadrature of f on [a, b] with n (even) panels."""
    if n % 2 == 1:
        n += 1
    if b == a:
        return 0.0
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += (4.0 if i % 2 == 1 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3.0


def bin_avg(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, w: float) -> float:
    """avg(f; a, w) = (1/w) * integral of f over [a, a + w]."""
    return integrate(f, a, a + w) / w


def bin_center(o: float, w: float, i: int) -> float:
    """Centre c_i(o, w) = o + (i + 1/2) w of the i-th bin of the grid (o, w)."""
    return o + (i + 0.5) * w


def bin_value(f: Callable[[float], float], o: float, w: float, i: int) -> float:
    """Bar height B_i(o, w) = avg(f; o + i w, w)."""
    return bin_avg(f, o + i * w, w)


def sliding_avg(f: Callable[[float], float], w: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Box-kernel sliding average (S_w f)(x) = (1/w) * integral over [x-w/2, x+w/2]."""
    return integrate(f, x - w / 2.0, x + w / 2.0) / w


def histogram(
    f: Callable[[float], float], n_bins: int, shift_in_bins: float
) -> Tuple[List[float], List[float]]:
    """Histogram f on the unit window with `n_bins` bins, grid shifted by
    `shift_in_bins` bin-widths.  Returns (bar heights, absolute bin centres)."""
    w = 1.0 / n_bins
    o = shift_in_bins * w
    heights = [bin_value(f, o, w, i) for i in range(n_bins)]
    centers = [bin_center(o, w, i) for i in range(n_bins)]
    return heights, centers


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The three-point local quadratic fit.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def q_vertex(x0: float, w: float, ym: float, y0: float, yp: float) -> float:
    """Vertex abscissa of the parabola through (x0-w, ym), (x0, y0), (x0+w, yp)."""
    d = ym - 2.0 * y0 + yp
    return x0 + w * (ym - yp) / (2.0 * d)


def q_peak(ym: float, y0: float, yp: float) -> float:
    """Vertex ordinate (fitted amplitude) of the same parabola."""
    d = ym - 2.0 * y0 + yp
    return y0 - (yp - ym) ** 2 / (8.0 * d)

def demo_sampling_identity() -> None:
    banner("1. SAMPLING IDENTITY:  B_i(o,w) = (S_w f)(c_i(o,w))")
    worst = 0.0
    for n_bins in BIN_COUNTS:

            w = 1.0 / n_bins
            o = sh * w
            for i in (0, n_bins // 3, n_bins // 2, n_bins - 1):

                rhs = sliding_avg(ratio_curve, w, bin_center(o, w, i))

def lipschitz_constant(f: Callable[[float], float], n: int = 20000) -> float:
    """Numerical sup |f'| on [0, 1] by finite differences."""
    h = 1.0 / n
    return max(abs(f((i + 1) * h) - f(i * h)) / h for i in range(n))

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple


def simpson(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, panels: int = 2048) -> float:
    """Composite Simpson quadrature of f on [a, b].  O(panels) evaluations."""
    if panels % 2 == 1:
        panels += 1
    if b == a:
        return 0.0
    h = (b - a) / panels
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, panels):
        total += (4.0 if i % 2 == 1 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3.0


def sliding_avg(f: Callable[[float], float], w: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Box-kernel sliding average of f at scale w, evaluated at x."""
    return simpson(f, x - w / 2.0, x + w / 2.0) / w


def bin_value(f: Callable[[float], float], o: float, w: float, i: int) -> float:
    """Height of the i-th bar of the grid with offset o and width w."""
    return simpson(f, o + i * w, o + i * w + w) / w


def bin_center(o: float, w: float, i: int) -> float:
    """Absolute centre of the i-th bin of the grid with offset o and width w."""
    return o + (i + 0.5) * w


def reduce_probe_grid(

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple


def simpson(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, panels: int = 2048) -> float:
    """Composite Simpson quadrature of f on [a, b]."""
    if panels % 2 == 1:
        panels += 1
    if b == a:
        return 0.0
    h = (b - a) / panels
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, panels):
        total += (4.0 if i % 2 == 1 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3.0


def flat_fwer(p: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Family-wise error of a bin-count-agnostic bar: 1 - (1-p)^n."""
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - p) ** n


def aware_fwer(alpha: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Family-wise error of the aware bar with per-bin level alpha/n."""
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha / n) ** n


def normal_quantile(q: float) -> float:
    """Inverse standard normal CDF (Acklam-style rational approximation)."""
    a = [-3.969683028665376e+01, 2.209460984245205e+02, -2.759285104469687e+02,
         1.383577518672690e+02, -3.066479806614716e+01, 2.506628277459239e+00]
    b = [-5.447609879822406e+01, 1.615858368580409e+02, -1.556989798598866e+02,
         6.680131188771972e+01, -1.328068155288572e+01]
    c = [-7.784894002430293e-03, -3.223964580411365e-01, -2.400758277161838e+00,
         -2.549732539343734e+00, 4.374664141464968e+00, 2.938163982698783e+00]
    d = [7.784695709041462e-03, 3.224671290700398e-01, 2.445134137142996e+00,
         3.754408661907416e+00]
    plow, phigh = 0.02425, 1.0 - 0.02425
    if q < plow:
        t = math.sqrt(-2.0 * math.log(q))
        return (((((c[0]*t+c[1])*t+c[2])*t+c[3])*t+c[4])*t+c[5]) / \
               ((((d[0]*t+d[1])*t+d[2])*t+d[3])*t+1.0)
    if q > phigh:
        t = math.sqrt(-2.0 * math.log(1.0 - q))
        return -(((((c[0]*t+c[1])*t+c[2])*t+c[3])*t+c[4])*t+c[5]) / \
                ((((d[0]*t+d[1])*t+d[2])*t+d[3])*t+1.0)
    t = q - 0.5
    r = t * t
    return (((((a[0]*r+a[1])*r+a[2])*r+a[3])*r+a[4])*r+a[5]) * t / \
           (((((b[0]*r+b[1])*r+b[2])*r+b[3])*r+b[4])*r+1.0)


def aware_amplitude_ceiling(n_bins: int, alpha: float, rel_sigma: float) -> float:
    """Amplitude ceiling for a ratio curve binned into n_bins bins.

    Under a uniform-sampling null each bar is approximately 1 + sigma * Z with
    sigma = rel_sigma / sqrt(count-per-bin) scaling; the two-sided aware level is
    alpha / n_bins, giving the extreme-value ceiling below.
    """
    z = normal_quantile(1.0 - alpha / (2.0 * n_bins))
    return 1.0 + z * rel_sigma * math.sqrt(float(n_bins))

    f: Callable[[float], float],

    shifts_in_bins: Sequence[float],

    rel_sigma: float = 0.0015,

def three_point_fit(
    x0: float, w: float, ym: float, y0: float, yp: float
) -> Dict[str, Optional[float]]:
    """Fit the parabola through the three points and classify the fit.

    Returns curvature, asymmetry, a degeneracy flag, and the vertex/amplitude,
    with the vertex set to None whenever it cannot be certified.
    Complexity: O(1).
    """
    d = ym - 2.0 * y0 + yp
    a = ym - yp
    if d >= 0.0:
        return {"curvature": d, "asymmetry": a, "degenerate": True,
                "vertex": None, "amplitude": None,
                "reason": "fit not strictly concave"}
    if abs(a) > -d:
        return {"curvature": d, "asymmetry": a, "degenerate": True,
                "vertex": None, "amplitude": y0 - (yp - ym) ** 2 / (8.0 * d),
                "reason": "asymmetry exceeds curvature: |A| > |D|"}
    return {"curvature": d, "asymmetry": a, "degenerate": False,
            "vertex": x0 + w * a / (2.0 * d),
            "amplitude": y0 - (yp - ym) ** 2 / (8.0 * d),
            "reason": "certified: |vertex - x0| <= w/2"}


def estimate_peak(
    bars: Sequence[float], centers: Sequence[float], w: float
) -> Dict[str, object]:

      1. locate the argmax bar (interior bars only, so neighbours exist);
      2. attempt the certified three-point fit;

         guaranteed within w/2 + (L/kappa) w of the true peak for every offset.

    Complexity: O(n_bins).

    n = len(bars)
    if n < 3:
        raise ValueError("need at least three bars")
    j = max(range(1, n - 1), key=lambda i: bars[i])
    fit = three_point_fit(centers[j], w, bars[j - 1], bars[j], bars[j + 1])
    used_fit = fit["vertex"] is not None
    return {
        "argmax_index": j,
        "argmax_center": centers[j],
        "raw_amplitude": bars[j],
        "fitted_amplitude": fit["amplitude"],
        "reported_vertex": fit["vertex"] if used_fit else centers[j],
        "vertex_source": "quadratic fit" if used_fit else "argmax bin centre",
        "degenerate": fit["degenerate"],
        "reason": fit["reason"],
        "curvature": fit["curvature"],
        "asymmetry": fit["asymmetry"],
        "half_bin": w / 2.0,
    }

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence


def bars_of(
    f: Callable[[float], float], n_bins: int, shift_in_bins: float, panels: int = 512
) -> List[float]:
    """Histogram bar heights of f on the unit window.  O(n_bins * panels)."""
    w = 1.0 / n_bins
    o = shift_in_bins * w

    def avg(a: float, b: float) -> float:
        h = (b - a) / panels
        s = f(a) + f(b)
        for i in range(1, panels):
            s += (4.0 if i % 2 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
        return s * h / 3.0 / (b - a)

    return [avg(o + i * w, o + i * w + w) for i in range(n_bins)]


def second_differences(bars: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Discrete curvature of the bar sequence.  O(n)."""
    return [bars[i + 1] - 2.0 * bars[i] + bars[i - 1] for i in range(1, len(bars) - 1)]


def curvature_sign_test(
    f: Callable[[float], float],
    bin_counts: Sequence[int],
    shifts_in_bins: Sequence[float],
    window: tuple[float, float],
) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Aggregate the curvature-sign certificate over a probe grid.

    For each cell, restrict to bars whose centres lie inside `window` and count
    how many have negative discrete curvature.  A genuine concave hump gives a
    high fraction at every width and offset; a binning artefact does not, because
    it has no consistent curvature sign across offsets.

    Complexity: O(|widths| * |shifts| * n_bins * panels).
    """
    lo, hi = window
    cells: List[Dict[str, object]] = []
    for n_bins in bin_counts:
        w = 1.0 / n_bins
        for sh in shifts_in_bins:
            o = sh * w
            bars = bars_of(f, n_bins, sh)
            d2 = second_differences(bars)
            inside = [k for k in range(len(d2))
                      if lo <= o + (k + 1 + 0.5) * w <= hi]
            if not inside:
                continue
            neg = sum(1 for k in inside if d2[k] < 0.0)
            cells.append({
                "n_bins": n_bins,
                "shift": sh,
                "bars_in_window": len(inside),
                "concave_fraction": neg / len(inside),
                "min_second_difference": min(d2[k] for k in inside),
            })
    fractions = [float(c["concave_fraction"]) for c in cells]
    return {
        "cells": cells,
        "min_concave_fraction": min(fractions),
        "mean_concave_fraction": sum(fractions) / len(fractions),
        "all_cells_concave": all(fr == 1.0 for fr in fractions),
    }

def ratio_curve(u: float) -> float:
    """Measured-to-modelled ratio with a mid-window hump at u* = 0.65."""
    return 1.0 + 0.23 * math.exp(-0.5 * ((u - U_STAR) / 0.16) ** 2)


def bin_average(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, panels: int = 256) -> float:
    """Simpson average of f over [a, b]."""
    h = (b - a) / panels
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, panels):
        s += (4.0 if i % 2 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return s * h / 3.0 / (b - a)


def histogram(
    f: Callable[[float], float], n_bins: int, shift: float
) -> Tuple[List[float], List[float], List[float]]:
    """Return (left edges, bar heights, bin centres) for the shifted grid."""
    w = 1.0 / n_bins
    o = shift * w
    edges = [o + i * w for i in range(n_bins)]
    bars = [bin_average(f, e, e + w) for e in edges]
    centers = [e + w / 2.0 for e in edges]
    return edges, bars, centers


def make_figure(
    bin_counts: Sequence[int] = (10, 20, 33, 50, 66, 100),
    shifts: Sequence[float] = (-0.25, -0.125, 0.0, 0.125, 0.25),
    filename: str = "thirty_views.png",
) -> None:
    """Draw the full probe grid."""
    xs = [k / 1000.0 for k in range(1001)]
    ys = [ratio_curve(x) for x in xs]
    true_sup = max(ys)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(bin_counts), len(shifts),
                             figsize=(15, 13), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for r, n_bins in enumerate(bin_counts):
        w = 1.0 / n_bins
        for c, sh in enumerate(shifts):
            ax = axes[r][c]
            edges, bars, centers = histogram(ratio_curve, n_bins, sh)
            ax.bar(edges, bars, width=w, align="edge",
                   color="#9ec5fe", edgecolor="#3b6fb6", linewidth=0.3)
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color="#c0392b", linewidth=1.4)
            j = max(range(len(bars)), key=lambda i: bars[i])
            ax.axvline(centers[j], color="#1b5e20", linestyle="-", linewidth=1.6)
            ax.axvline(U_STAR, color="#000000", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.2)
            ax.axhline(true_sup, color="#7f8c8d", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
            ax.set_xlim(0.30, 1.0)
            ax.set_ylim(0.95, 1.28)
            ax.text(0.32, 1.245,
                    f"n={n_bins}, sh={sh:+.3f}\nlabel {j} -> centre {centers[j]:.4f}",
                    fontsize=7.5, va="top")
            if r == len(bin_counts) - 1:
                ax.set_xlabel("u")
            if c == 0:
                ax.set_ylabel("R = T/M")

    fig.suptitle(
        "Thirty views of one hump: bin width x grid shift\n"
        "green = absolute centre of the tallest bar   dotted = true peak u* = 0.65"
        "   dashed = true supremum",
        fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.955))
    fig.savefig(filename, dpi=140)
    print(f"wrote {filename}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    make_figure()

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

U_STAR: float = 0.65
C_PEAK: float = 1.23
K_CURV: float = 4.0


def parabola(x: float) -> float:
    """The canonical hump f(x) = c - k (x - x*)^2."""
    return C_PEAK - K_CURV * (x - U_STAR) ** 2


def gaussian_hump(x: float) -> float:
    """A smooth, nearly-symmetric hump used for the transport panel."""
    return 1.0 + 0.23 * math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - U_STAR) / 0.16) ** 2)


def sliding_avg(f: Callable[[float], float], w: float, x: float, panels: int = 512) -> float:
    """Box-kernel sliding average of f at scale w evaluated at x."""
    a, b = x - w / 2.0, x + w / 2.0
    h = (b - a) / panels
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, panels):
        s += (4.0 if i % 2 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return s * h / 3.0 / w


def make_figure(filename: str = "invariance_diagnostics.png") -> None:
    bin_counts: Sequence[int] = (10, 20, 33, 50, 66, 100)
    shifts: Sequence[float] = (-0.25, -0.125, 0.0, 0.125, 0.25)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 10))

    # (a) deflation law
    ax = axes[0][0]
    w2 = [(1.0 / n) ** 2 for n in bin_counts]
    measured = [sliding_avg(parabola, 1.0 / n, U_STAR) for n in bin_counts]
    predicted = [C_PEAK - K_CURV * v / 12.0 for v in w2]
    ax.plot(w2, measured, "o", color="#c0392b", label="measured peak of box average")
    ax.plot(w2, predicted, "-", color="#2c3e50", label="c - k w^2 / 12 (exact)")
    ax.set_xlabel("w^2")
    ax.set_ylabel("peak amplitude")
    ax.set_title("(a) exact amplitude deflation, no offset dependence")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # (b) label drift vs absolute invariance
    ax = axes[0][1]
    for n in (20, 50, 100):
        w = 1.0 / n
        labels: List[float] = []
        centres: List[float] = []
        for sh in shifts:
            o = sh * w
            bars = [sliding_avg(gaussian_hump, w, o + (i + 0.5) * w) for i in range(n)]
            j = max(range(n), key=lambda i: bars[i])
            labels.append(j / n)
            centres.append(o + (j + 0.5) * w)
        ax.plot(shifts, labels, "--o", label=f"label/n, n={n}")
        ax.plot(shifts, centres, "-s", label=f"absolute centre, n={n}")
    ax.axhline(U_STAR, color="black", linestyle=":", label="true peak u*")
    ax.set_xlabel("grid shift (bin widths)")
    ax.set_ylabel("reported location")
    ax.set_title("(b) labels drift, absolute centres are pinned")
    ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=2)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # (c) shape preservation
    ax = axes[1][0]
    xs = [0.30 + 0.7 * k / 600.0 for k in range(601)]
    ax.plot(xs, [gaussian_hump(x) for x in xs], color="black", linewidth=2,

    for n, colour in zip((10, 20, 50), ("#c0392b", "#e67e22", "#2980b9")):
        w = 1.0 / n
        ax.plot(xs, [sliding_avg(gaussian_hump, w, x) for x in xs], color=colour,
                linewidth=1.3, label=f"box average, w = 1/{n}")
    ax.axvline(U_STAR, color="gray", linestyle=":")
    ax.set_xlabel("u")
    ax.set_ylabel("value")
    ax.set_title("(c) box averaging lowers the peak but does not move it")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # (d) threshold audit
    ax = axes[1][1]
    ns = list(range(2, 401))
    for p, colour in ((0.005, "#8e44ad"), (0.01, "#c0392b"), (0.02, "#e67e22")):
        ax.plot(ns, [1.0 - (1.0 - p) ** n for n in ns], color=colour,

    ax.plot(ns, [1.0 - (1.0 - 0.05 / n) ** n for n in ns], color="#27ae60",

    ax.axhline(0.05, color="black", linestyle=":", label="alpha = 0.05")
    ax.set_xlabel("number of bins n")
    ax.set_ylabel("family-wise error")
    ax.set_title("(d) a flat bar loses control; the aware bar does not")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(filename, dpi=140)
    print(f"wrote {filename}")

<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";

  const U_STAR = 0.65;
  const BASE = 1.0, PEAK = 0.23;

  const el = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
  const cv = el("plot"), ctx = cv.getContext("2d");

  function curve(u, sigma, skew) {
    const z = (u - U_STAR) / sigma;
    const g = Math.exp(-0.5 * z * z);
    // skewed Gaussian: multiply by a smooth monotone tilt, still a single hump
    const tilt = 1.0 + skew * Math.tanh(z);
    return BASE + PEAK * g * Math.max(0.0, tilt);
  }

  function binAvg(f, a, b, panels) {
    panels = panels || 64;
    const h = (b - a) / panels;
    let s = f(a) + f(b);
    for (let i = 1; i < panels; i++) s += (i % 2 ? 4 : 2) * f(a + i * h);
    return s * h / 3 / (b - a);
  }

  function state() {
    const nb = +el("nb").value;
    const sh = +el("sh").value / 200;      // -0.25 .. +0.25
    const sigma = +el("sg").value / 100;
    const skew = +el("sk").value / 100;
    const bar = +el("tb").value / 100;
    return { nb, sh, sigma, skew, bar };
  }

  function compute(st) {
    const f = (u) => curve(u, st.sigma, st.skew);
    const w = 1 / st.nb, o = st.sh * w;
    const bars = [], centers = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < st.nb; i++) {
      const a = o + i * w;
      bars.push(binAvg(f, a, a + w));
      centers.push(a + w / 2);
    }
    let j = 0;
    for (let i = 1; i < bars.length; i++) if (bars[i] > bars[j]) j = i;

    // true supremum and its location, by dense scan
    let sup = -Infinity, xsup = 0;
    for (let k = 0; k <= 4000; k++) {
      const x = k / 4000, v = f(x);
      if (v > sup) { sup = v; xsup = x; }
    }

    // three-point fit at the argmax bar (interior only)
    let fit = null;
    if (j > 0 && j < st.nb - 1) {
      const ym = bars[j - 1], y0 = bars[j], yp = bars[j + 1];
      const D = ym - 2 * y0 + yp, A = ym - yp;
      const concave = D < 0;
      const apex = concave ? y0 - Math.pow(yp - ym, 2) / (8 * D) : null;
      const vx = concave ? centers[j] + w * A / (2 * D) : null;
      fit = { ym, y0, yp, D, A, concave,
              degenerate: !concave || Math.abs(A) > -D,
              apex, vx };
    }
    return { f, w, o, bars, centers, j, sup, xsup, fit };
  }

  // ---- drawing -----------------------------------------------------------
  const M = { l: 70, r: 24, t: 26, b: 52 };
  const XMIN = 0.15, XMAX = 1.0, YMIN = 0.96;

  function draw(st, c) {
    const W = cv.width, H = cv.height;
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    const ymax = Math.max(1.30, c.sup + 0.04);
    const X = (u) => M.l + (u - XMIN) / (XMAX - XMIN) * (W - M.l - M.r);
    const Y = (v) => H - M.b - (v - YMIN) / (ymax - YMIN) * (H - M.t - M.b);

    // grid
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#eef2f7"; ctx.lineWidth = 1;
    for (let g = 0; g <= 10; g++) {
      const u = XMIN + g * (XMAX - XMIN) / 10;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(u), M.t); ctx.lineTo(X(u), H - M.b); ctx.stroke();
    }
    for (let g = 0; g <= 6; g++) {
      const v = YMIN + g * (ymax - YMIN) / 6;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(M.l, Y(v)); ctx.lineTo(W - M.r, Y(v)); ctx.stroke();
    }
    // axes
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#8d9aa8"; ctx.lineWidth = 1.4;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(M.l, M.t); ctx.lineTo(M.l, H - M.b);
    ctx.lineTo(W - M.r, H - M.b); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillStyle = "#5b6b7c"; ctx.font = "16px monospace";
    for (let g = 0; g <= 10; g++) {
      const u = XMIN + g * (XMAX - XMIN) / 10;
      ctx.fillText(u.toFixed(2), X(u) - 16, H - M.b + 24);
    }
    for (let g = 0; g <= 6; g++) {
      const v = YMIN + g * (ymax - YMIN) / 6;
      ctx.fillText(v.toFixed(2), 14, Y(v) + 5);
    }
    ctx.fillText("u", (W) / 2, H - 12);

    // bars
    for (let i = 0; i < c.bars.length; i++) {
      const a = c.o + i * c.w;
      if (a + c.w < XMIN || a > XMAX) continue;
      const x0 = X(Math.max(a, XMIN)), x1 = X(Math.min(a + c.w, XMAX));
      ctx.fillStyle = (i === c.j) ? "#6fa8f5" : "#cfe1fb";
      ctx.fillRect(x0, Y(c.bars[i]), Math.max(1, x1 - x0), Y(YMIN) - Y(c.bars[i]));
      ctx.strokeStyle = "#3b6fb6"; ctx.lineWidth = 0.6;
      ctx.strokeRect(x0, Y(c.bars[i]), Math.max(1, x1 - x0), Y(YMIN) - Y(c.bars[i]));
    }

    // sliding average (box-averaged curve)
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#e67e22"; ctx.lineWidth = 2; ctx.beginPath();
    for (let k = 0; k <= 400; k++) {
      const u = XMIN + k * (XMAX - XMIN) / 400;
      const v = binAvg(c.f, u - c.w / 2, u + c.w / 2, 24);
      if (k === 0) ctx.moveTo(X(u), Y(v)); else ctx.lineTo(X(u), Y(v));
    }
    ctx.stroke();

    // true curve
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#c0392b"; ctx.lineWidth = 2.6; ctx.beginPath();
    for (let k = 0; k <= 800; k++) {
      const u = XMIN + k * (XMAX - XMIN) / 800;
      const v = c.f(u);
      if (k === 0) ctx.moveTo(X(u), Y(v)); else ctx.lineTo(X(u), Y(v));
    }
    ctx.stroke();

    // supremum line
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#95a5a6"; ctx.setLineDash([7, 6]); ctx.lineWidth = 1.4;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(M.l, Y(c.sup)); ctx.lineTo(W - M.r, Y(c.sup)); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);

    // amplitude bar
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#8e44ad"; ctx.setLineDash([3, 5]);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(M.l, Y(st.bar)); ctx.lineTo(W - M.r, Y(st.bar)); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#8e44ad"; ctx.font = "15px monospace";
    ctx.fillText("amplitude bar " + st.bar.toFixed(2), W - M.r - 210, Y(st.bar) - 8);

    // true peak
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#000"; ctx.setLineDash([2, 4]); ctx.lineWidth = 1.6;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(c.xsup), M.t); ctx.lineTo(X(c.xsup), H - M.b); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);

    // absolute centre of argmax bar
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#1b5e20"; ctx.lineWidth = 2.4;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(c.centers[c.j]), M.t);
    ctx.lineTo(X(c.centers[c.j]), H - M.b); ctx.stroke();

    // fitted apex
    if (c.fit && c.fit.vx !== null && isFinite(c.fit.vx)) {
      ctx.strokeStyle = c.fit.degenerate ? "#b3261e" : "#8e44ad";
      ctx.lineWidth = 2; ctx.setLineDash([6, 4]);
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(X(Math.max(XMIN, Math.min(XMAX, c.fit.vx))), M.t);
      ctx.lineTo(X(Math.max(XMIN, Math.min(XMAX, c.fit.vx))), H - M.b);
      ctx.stroke(); ctx.setLineDash([]);

  "interactive_layout": "# Is the bump real? A guided tour of binning-independent geometry

> **The question.** You plot a ratio curve $R(u) = T(u)/M(u)$ — measurement over model —
> on a normalised window $u \in [0,1]$. If the model were perfect, $R$ would sit flat at
> $1$. Instead there is a broad hump near $u^{*} \approx 0.65$, rising to about $1.2$.
> Before you write a word about it, you have to answer one thing: **is that bump in the
> data, or in the picture?**

A histogram has two knobs — how wide the bins are, and where the grid starts. Turn either
and the picture changes. This page works out, precisely, which features of a bump are
immune to those knobs and which are hostages to them. By the end you will be able to say
which of your own histogram readouts are facts about the world and which are facts about
your plotting choices.

---

## 1. Play first, theory second

Here is one curve and every histogram you could draw of it. Drag the sliders. Watch two
numbers in particular: the **label** of the tallest bar and its **absolute centre**.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>What you should have noticed (open after playing)</b></summary>

1. **The label moves; the absolute position does not.** As you slide the grid, the index
   of the winning bar jumps around, but its absolute centre stays glued near $0.65$,
   never straying more than half a bin from the true peak.
2. **No bar ever pokes above the true supremum.** Averaging pulls values toward the mean;
   it cannot create height.
3. **More bins, taller bars.** The peak deficit shrinks as the bins narrow — and for a
   parabolic hump it shrinks *exactly* like $k w^2 / 12$.
4. **The parabola fit can go crazy.** Crank the skew slider and the fitted apex flies off
   the chart while the argmax bar stays exactly where it was.

Every one of those four observations is a theorem. Let us prove them.
</details>

---

## 2. The idea that dissolves the problem

A histogram bar is an average. For a bin running from $a$ to $a+w$,

$$ \operatorname{avg}(f;a,w) \;=\; \frac{1}{w}\int_a^{a+w} f(x)\,dx . $$

A grid $(o,w)$ has bars $B_i(o,w) = \operatorname{avg}(f; o+iw, w)$ at centres
$c_i(o,w) = o + (i+\tfrac12)w$. Now define a function with no grid in it at all — the
**box-kernel sliding average**:

$$ (S_w f)(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{w}\int_{x-w/2}^{x+w/2} f(s)\,ds . $$

> **Sampling Identity.** $B_i(o,w) = (S_w f)\big(c_i(o,w)\big)$ for every $o$, $w$, $i$.

Both sides are $1/w$ times the integral of $f$ over the *same* interval of length $w$.
That is the whole proof, and it reorganises everything: **the offset is not a parameter of
the statistic**. Thirty histograms are not thirty statistics — they are six smoothed
copies of one curve, sampled at five sets of points each. The bin width picks the copy;
the offset picks only where you stand.

<details>
<summary><b>Two immediate corollaries: why labels must drift</b></summary>

Shifting the *data* by $t$ and shifting the *grid* by $t$ are literally the same
operation, because Lebesgue measure is translation invariant:
$\operatorname{avg}(f(\cdot+t);a,w) = \operatorname{avg}(f;a+t,w)$. Meanwhile bin centres
move rigidly: $c_i(o+t,w) = c_i(o,w) + t$.

So under a grid shift the winning bin's *index* must change by construction, and the
quantity "index plus shift" — the absolute position — is the only thing that can be
invariant. Anyone who compares raw bin labels across shifts and reports the difference as
instability is reporting a theorem as a bug.
</details>

---

## 3. Binning cannot invent a hump

> **One-Sided Certificate.** If any bar of any histogram — any width, any offset — has
> height at least $c$, then the curve genuinely attains at least $c$ somewhere in that bin.

*Proof.* An average over an interval never exceeds the maximum over that interval, and a
continuous function on a closed interval attains its maximum. $\blacksquare$

Binning is *lossy in one direction only*: it can flatten a spike into invisibility, but it
can never manufacture height. So "the hump appears in every cell of the grid" is not even
an artefact hypothesis — there is nothing to refute. Only the *calibration* of the
amplitude is open.

{{algorithm:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why this changes how you should read a robustness check</b></summary>

The folk rule is "vary the bin width; if the feature survives, believe it". The certificate
tells you exactly *why* that rule is sound for existence claims, and exactly where it stops
being sound: survival certifies a lower bound for $\sup f$, and nothing more. Whether that
lower bound is *surprising* is a question for the null model, not for the binning — which
is the subject of section 6.
</details>

---

## 4. Amplitude: stable, and computably biased

Suppose $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, so $|f(x)-f(y)| \le L|x-y|$. If the true maximiser $x_s$
falls in the bin $[a,a+w]$, then

$$ \big|\operatorname{avg}(f;a,w) - f(x_s)\big| \;\le\; L\,w. $$

Averaging can only deflate the peak, and not by more than the curve can fall across one bin.
Hence:

> **Width Independence.** Two grids of widths $w_1, w_2$ and *arbitrary, unrelated* offsets
> each contain a bin whose height is within $L(w_1+w_2)$ of the other's.

For the canonical smooth hump the worst-case bound becomes an identity. Take
$f(s) = c - k(s-x_s)^2$. Then

$$ (S_w f)(x) \;=\; c - k\Big[(x-x_s)^2 + \frac{w^2}{12}\Big]. $$

The parabola comes back *verbatim*: same curvature, same vertex. The only effect of the bin
width is a uniform drop of exactly $k w^2/12$, with no offset anywhere in the formula. Two
widths differ by exactly $k(w_2^2 - w_1^2)/12$ — a deterministic bias you can simply
subtract, not evidence against a feature.

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Sketch of the parabola computation</b></summary>

Split the integral. The constant contributes $c$. For the quadratic part use
$\int_a^b (s-d)^2\,ds = \frac{(b-d)^3-(a-d)^3}{3}$ with $a = x - w/2$, $b = x + w/2$,
$d = x_s$, $\delta = x - x_s$; the cubes expand to $w\delta^2 + w^3/12$. Divide by $w$.
The cross terms cancel because the window is *centred* — which is precisely the content of
the sampling identity.
</details>

---

## 5. Position: rigid transport

How far can the winning bin be from the true peak? Two answers, one general and one sharp.

**General.** Ask only that the peak be a genuine peak, quantitatively: a *cone condition*
$f(x) \le f(x_s) - \kappa|x-x_s|$. Then for **any** offset and width, any bin beating the
bin that contains $x_s$ has centre within

$$ \frac{w}{2} + \frac{L}{\kappa}\,w $$

of $x_s$. There is no $o$ in that bound. Slide the grid however you like; the winner's
absolute centre stays in a fixed window around the truth, and refining the bins closes it.

**Sharp.** Box averaging is *shape-preserving*: it preserves reflection symmetry about a
point, and it preserves concavity. A symmetric concave function is radially monotone — its
value depends only monotonically on distance from the centre — and that property is
inherited by the smoothed copy. Therefore:

> **Exact Rigid Transport.** If $f$ is symmetric about $x_s$ and concave, then for every
> bin width the sliding average peaks *exactly* at $x_s$; every bar of every grid is capped
> by the single number $(S_w f)(x_s)$; and for every offset the winning bar is precisely
> the one whose centre is nearest $x_s$.

No slack, no offset, no fitting. The argmax bin is chosen by pure geometry.

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Proof of radial monotonicity (the one non-obvious step)</b></summary>

Let $g$ be symmetric about $x_s$ and concave, and suppose $|u - x_s| \le |v - x_s|$. Write
$t = v - x_s$ and $r = u - x_s$. If $t = 0$ then $r = 0$ and there is nothing to prove.
Otherwise $|r/t| \le 1$, so $\lambda = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{r}{2t}$ lies in $[0,1]$ and
$$ \lambda(x_s + t) + (1-\lambda)(x_s - t) = u . $$
Concavity gives $\lambda g(x_s+t) + (1-\lambda)g(x_s-t) \le g(u)$, and symmetry gives
$g(x_s - t) = g(x_s + t) = g(v)$. The left-hand side is therefore just $g(v)$, so
$g(v) \le g(u)$. $\blacksquare$

Read [convex/concave function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concave_function) and
[unimodality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodality) if these notions are new.
</details>

---

## 6. Where the pipeline actually broke

So far every result has been about the *curve*. The two remaining puzzles are about the
*instrument* — and both turn out to be mis-specifications rather than discoveries.

### 6a. The smoothing fit is not conservative

Fit a parabola through three consecutive bars $(y_-, y_0, y_+)$ at spacing $w$. Write the
discrete curvature $D = y_- - 2y_0 + y_+$ and the neighbour asymmetry $A = y_- - y_+$.
The apex sits at

$$ \hat{x} = x_0 + \frac{wA}{2D}, \qquad \hat{y} = y_0 - \frac{(y_+-y_-)^2}{8D} . $$

If the fit is genuinely concave ($D < 0$) then the subtracted term is negative, so
$\hat y \ge y_0$ — **always**. Fitting can only *raise* the reported amplitude. An
amplitude bar on the fitted apex is therefore *easier* to clear than the same bar on the
raw bar height, not harder. Anyone who adopted the fit believing it was the cautious
choice had it backwards.

And if the centre bar dominates its neighbours, $|\hat x - x_0| \le w/2$: the apex stays
within half a bin. Contrapositively, **a vertex further away than half a bin proves
$|A| > |D|$** — the asymmetry beat the curvature, the denominator was nearly zero, the fit
was ill-conditioned. A far-flung vertex is a certificate about the arithmetic, not about
the feature.

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>The degeneracy certificate, in one line</b></summary>

With $D<0$ and $-D = 2y_0 - y_- - y_+$, note $-D - A = 2(y_0 - y_-)$ and
$-D + A = 2(y_0 - y_+)$. So $y_\pm \le y_0$ is *equivalent* to $|A| \le -D$, and in that
case $|wA/(2D)| = w|A|/(2|D|) \le w/2$. Turn it around: a vertex outside the half-bin
window forces $|A| > |D|$. Filtering on $|A| \le |D|$ before trusting a vertex costs one
comparison and removes the entire failure mode.
</details>

### 6b. A control bar must know how many bins it faces

Suppose each of $n$ bins independently exceeds a fixed level with probability $p>0$. Then
the chance that *at least one* does is $1 - (1-p)^n \to 1$. A bin-count-agnostic threshold
is therefore **guaranteed** to be breached once the grid is fine enough — by refinement
alone, with no signal in the data. The fix is the bin-count-aware bar with per-bin level
$\alpha/n$, for which Bernoulli's inequality gives

$$ 1 - \Big(1 - \frac{\alpha}{n}\Big)^n \;\le\; \alpha \qquad \text{for every } n . $$

Explore both, and simulate null grids to watch the flat bar fail:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why the breaches at the finest binnings were expected</b></summary>

If the finest three grids ($n = 50, 66, 100$) are the only ones to breach a flat bar, that
pattern is itself the tell: a genuine contamination would not preferentially target high
$n$, whereas the extreme value of $n$ independent-ish bin counts grows like
$\sqrt{2\log n}$ standard deviations. Breaches at $z \approx 3$ in the finest grids are the
null behaving normally. Read up on the
[family-wise error rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family-wise_error_rate) and the
[Šidák correction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%A0id%C3%A1k_correction), which is
exactly the $1 - (1-\alpha/n)^n$ bound above.
</details>

---

## 7. A test with no free parameters at all

If a fitted curvature can go degenerate, do not fit a curvature. The second difference of
three consecutive bars,

$$ B_{i+1} - 2B_i + B_{i-1}, $$

is non-positive for a concave curve at **every** bin width and **every** offset — a direct
consequence of the fact that box averaging preserves concavity, plus the observation that
consecutive bin centres are exactly one bin width apart. No denominator, no apex, nothing
to become ill-conditioned. Curvature sign, read straight off the bars.

{{algorithm:3}}

---

Everything above, end to end, on a synthetic hump: the sampling identity, the certificate,
amplitude stability, the exact deflation law, vertex transport, the fit audit, the control
audit, and the full grid table.

## 9. What to take away

| Readout | Depends on the offset? | Depends on the width? |
|---|---|---|
| A bar reaching height $c$ | no (certificate) | no |
| Amplitude | only through sampling | $O(Lw)$; exactly $kw^2/12$ for a parabola |
| Argmax bin **label** | **yes — by construction** | yes |
| Argmax bin **centre** | transports rigidly | within $w/2 + (L/\kappa)w$ of the peak |
| Sign of the second difference | no | no, for concave curves |
| Fitted apex height | inherits sampling; always $\ge$ raw | plus fit bias |
| Fitted apex position | degenerate when $\vert A\vert > \vert D\vert$ | as above |

The pattern is the moral. **Functionals with no free parameters are invariant, or
invariant up to a bias you can write down. Functionals the analyst adds — a fitted apex, a
flat threshold — are the ones that fail.** When a robustness check comes back mixed, the
first suspect should be the estimator, not the phenomenon.

<details>
<summary><b>Where this goes next</b></summary>

Two conjectures point beyond what is proved here.

*Curvature-sign certificates.* For $f \in C^2$, the second difference of bin averages
should equal $w \cdot (f'' \star \Lambda_w)(x)$ for the triangular (Bartlett) kernel
$\Lambda_w$ — making the histogram's discrete curvature an unbiased readout of the
smoothed sign pattern of $f''$, with an analytic error term and no fitted parameters at
all.

*Second-order vertex rigidity.* The symmetry hypothesis should weaken to log-concavity plus
a skew bound $|f(x_s+t) - f(x_s-t)| \le \varepsilon t^2$, yielding a vertex displacement of
order $\varepsilon w^2$ rather than $w$. The first-order term in the displacement of a box
average is exactly the local skewness, so a curve whose skewness vanishes to second order
should inherit *quadratic* rigidity — which would explain why observed vertex spreads come
out an order of magnitude tighter than the first-order prediction.

Combine either with a closed-form null variance and you get a significance test with no
bootstrap, no seed, and no fitted curvature: the honest replacement for the test that
failed.
</details>
